source: Xia et al. (2026) Who Broke the System? Failure Localization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems (AgentLocate)
finding: AgentLocate (COLM 2026) names an agent and the earliest decisive step in a failed multi-agent run. A judge LLM proposes one hypothesis, independent evaluators re-check it, and a confidence-weighted vote picks the answer. There is no hitting set, no conflict set and no tree. It is a single-hypothesis propose-then-verify design.
numbers: Benchmarks: Who&When (Algorithm-Generated and Hand-Crafted) and Aegis-Bench (9,533 failure trajectories). Best Who&When Algorithm-Generated agent-level accuracy 69.05% (Qwen-7B, both all-at-once and step-by-step); other models roughly 40% to 62%.
quote: a single attribution pass is often brittle for long, tool-mediated trajectories
limits: Small open models (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, Mistral-7B) plus GPT-4o; Who&When test split is only about 42 cases (40%), so one case is about 2.4 points. Step-level accuracy stays low (about 23% to 38%). Authors fine-tune the judge.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the 2026 failure-attribution line does not use a hitting-set formulation. It confirms that one-shot attribution is brittle and that independent re-checks of a named suspect help.

source: Xia et al. (2026) Who Broke the System? Failure Localization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems (AgentLocate) - evaluator ablation
finding: Adding independent evaluators to check a suspect hypothesis raised accuracy sharply from 1 to 3 evaluators, then flattened. One refinement round was enough.
numbers: Qwen-7B, Algorithm-Generated, all-at-once: agent-level 35.71% with 1 evaluator to 69.05% with 3; 5 or 7 evaluators gave no consistent further gain. Rounds 1 to 3: gains marginal and inconsistent. Poisoning-forensics baselines (RAGOrigin, RAGForensics) below 34% agent-level.
limits: Small test set; the 1-evaluator point is not the same as a plain judge baseline. Fine-tuned judge confounds the voting effect (Variant III, fine-tune on labels only, also scored below full system).
agent_relevance: A cheap rule for the suspect list: three independent checks of the leading suspect beat one, more than three add nothing. Useful as a budget cap in S5.

source: Ge et al. (2025) Who is Introducing the Failure? Automatically Attributing Failures of Multi-Agent Systems via Spectrum Analysis (Famas)
finding: Famas applies spectrum-based fault localization (Ochiai-style suspiciousness over repeated runs) to multi-agent traces. This is the classical SBFL branch of diagnosis, not the hitting-set branch. It needs many repeated executions of the same task.
numbers: Who&When, 184 failure logs: agent-level 57.61% (106/184), action-level 29.35% (54/184). Algorithm-generated (126 logs): 55.56% and 23.81%. Hand-crafted (58 logs): 62.07% (36/58) and 41.38% (24/58). Random baseline 23.71% agent / 14.36% action. Claims +49.13% relative action-level over the best LLM method (9.67/19.68 points).
limits: Preprint (v1). Needs repeated replays, so cost scales with runs. Action-level accuracy is still below 30% overall. Own re-implementation of 12 baselines.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: a ranking-by-suspiciousness formulation beats LLM-only attribution in this benchmark; no hitting set was used. Suggests counting evidence per suspect across runs can add what in-context judging lacks.

source: Ge et al. (2025) Who is Introducing the Failure? Automatically Attributing Failures of Multi-Agent Systems via Spectrum Analysis (Famas) - baselines and SBFL variants
finding: Swapping Famas's own scoring formula for classic SBFL formulas lowered accuracy; Tarantula was worst. Famas beat all LLM-judge baselines at both levels, even those given the ground-truth answer.
numbers: Famas beat the best SBFL variants (Famas-Ochiai, Famas-Kulczynski2) by 6.0% relative at agent level (3.26/54.35) and 35.0% relative at action level (7.61/21.74). Beat best LLM method (all-at-once with ground truth) by 5.5% at agent level.
limits: Authors designed the new formula and evaluated it on the same benchmark; no outside replication seen.
agent_relevance: Counting how often a step appears in failing vs passing runs is a cheap, code-side signal an LLM agent could use for suspect ranking.

source: Delta1 with LLM: symbolic and neural integration for credible and explainable reasoning (2026)
finding: Delta1-LLM uses an LLM only as front end (extract predicates) and back end (explain). A deterministic generator builds theorems that are minimally unsatisfiable by construction, so no MUS detector is run. It cites MARCO only as classical background.
numbers: No LLM-vs-baseline accuracy table found in the text read; the paper reports case studies and 24 non-equivalent formula-template cases.
limits: Not a verifier built on MARCO or any hitting-set duality. Evidence is demonstrative, not a measured benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the closest 2026 neuro-symbolic MUS paper does not use MARCO plus hitting sets as an LLM verifier. Keeps K22 (solver does the exact set work, LLM only verbalises) but adds no accuracy number.

source: Ijima and Yawata (2026) Hypergraph Neural Networks Accelerate MUS Enumeration (HyMUSE)
finding: A learned agent (hypergraph neural net, trained by reinforcement learning, not an LLM) chooses which constraints to shrink in MARCO-style MUS enumeration. It tracks MUSes found as hyperedges and uses hitting-set duality of MUSes and MSSes. Within a fixed budget of 10,000 satisfiability checks it enumerated more MUSes than plain MARCO.
numbers: Budget 10,000 satisfiability checks per method; reports the trained agent enumerates significantly more MUSes/MSSes than untrained agent and MARCO. Exact counts not extracted.
limits: Learned heuristic, not an LLM; MUS correctness is kept by an oracle correction step. Exact per-benchmark numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: shows hitting-set duality plus a learned chooser helps conflict-finding when checks are expensive. Direct support for a design where code keeps the exact set and the learned/LLM part only picks what to check next.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025) - code interpreter and model choice
finding: Only one run used a code tool: gpt-4o-mini with a Python interpreter. It was the worst model on MSO, conflict and diagnosis generation. Reasoning models (o1, o3-mini) without a visible tool did much better. Earlier tries with gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini gave accuracy 'close to zero on unseen examples'.
numbers: Models: gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 (with code interpreter), o3-mini-2025-01-31, o1-2024-12-17. 4o-mini and o3-mini each repeated 10 times per case; o1 once (about 30 USD per iteration). o3-mini F1 0.917 +/- 0.249 (conflicts), 0.784 +/- 0.322 (diagnoses).
quote: we cannot tell for sure that these models did not use a code interpreter in the background as well
limits: Not a controlled in-context vs tool comparison: the tool arm is also the weakest model. Authors cannot rule out hidden code use by o1 and o3-mini. Each step got gold input.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open as a controlled test, but the one data point says a weak model with a code tool did not beat a strong reasoning model in-context on these small instances. Tool offloading helps only if the model writes correct code for the exact step.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025) - difficulty trends
finding: Diagnosis generation (the minimal hitting set step) was the most computation-heavy task and showed a clear fall in F1 as the number of relations and diagnoses grew. Conflict generation looked like it improved with complexity, but only because the zero-conflict cases were the hard ones.
numbers: Prompts contained theory plus pseudo-code of the algorithm. Incidence matrix: o1 and o3-mini perfect accuracy; 4o-mini F1 0.47 +/- 0.15, accuracy 0.00. Dedicated and Broad prompt styles scored about the same despite more domain knowledge in Dedicated.
limits: Hand-built logic circuits, tens of components at most; gold inputs per step; OpenAI only. Exact breaking point (diagnosis count) is plotted in figures, not stated in text.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the LLM's own hitting-set step degrades with size even with gold conflicts. Argues for a code tool once conflict count or diagnosis count is large, but breakpoint is not measured.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025) - no head-to-head with a code tool
finding: The paper's conclusion says LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms and points to future hybrid frameworks and Model Context Protocol tool use. The exact hitting-set step was never given to a solver while the LLM did conflicts.
numbers: Reference diagnoses came from the Fault Diagnosis Toolbox and a minimal hitting set implementation. No equal-token comparison.
limits: Absence of evidence in this paper; a search for another study (one WebSearch) also found none.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answer: no equal-token measurement exists. We have to run it ourselves.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT) chooses the next question by expected information gain. The LLM proposes questions and simulates answer branches that split the current candidate set into yes and no groups. The entropy is then computed from set sizes in code, so the LLM never has to compute entropy itself. It beat direct prompting across medical diagnosis, troubleshooting and 20 Questions.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; +46.6% for Llama3-70B; beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, Original-ToT by 28.3%, Adapted-ToT by 12.4%. Simulation limited to 3 steps for cost.
limits: '38.1%' is an average of per-dataset gains, not one clean number. Answerer is an LLM (GPT-4) simulating the patient; simplified medical datasets (DX has 5 diseases).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a split-the-candidates rule (probability near 0.5) with set sizes counted outside the LLM works for an LLM chooser. Supports a split-in-half probe rule over exact entropy.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024) - per-task numbers
finding: Task-level results with GPT-4 in the closed-set setting: DX medical dataset 97.0% success; MedDG 88.0% (GPT-4), 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro); troubleshooting 67.3% vs 43.7% for direct prompting, with fewest questions (7.8). DX mean questions 2.0 vs 3.0 to 3.5.
numbers: DX: 104 doctor-patient dialogues, 5 diseases. Troubleshooting limited to 5 turns for closed-ended scenarios.
limits: Closed-set means the candidate list is given, which matches a known suspect list but not an open one. Open-set UoT was only about 8.7% better than Adapted-ToT on 20 Questions.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: gains hold when the candidate list is explicit, the situation closest to our suspect list.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024) - reward scaling ablation
finding: Plain expected information gain was about as good as log-scaled gain, and better than piecewise scaling on one dataset. The tuned reward that penalises uneven splits was kept.
numbers: Plain IG vs log vs sigmoid vs piecewise success rates: 20Q-BIG-bench 51.7/51.7/51.3/37.9; Common 41.4/40.5/35.1/36.9; DX 90.4/91.3/89.4/89.4; MedDG 81.1/78.0/82.3/81.3; FloDial 67.9/65.4/63.4/67.1.
limits: Differences of 1 to 3 points are inside noise for these dataset sizes; no repeated runs reported in the table.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the exact reward form barely matters; what matters is that the split is near even. A simple 'pick the test that halves the suspects' is probably enough.

source: Riddell et al. (2026) Stalled, Biased, and Confused: Uncovering Reasoning Failures in LLMs for Cloud-Based Root Cause Analysis
finding: A controlled study of LLM root-cause analysis found accuracy low across models and workflows. Anchoring, repetition and failure to update belief predicted wrong answers. The authors restricted every scenario to one known fault and say concurrent faults are a limitation.
numbers: Reasoning-failure rates were high across models; agentic workflows often gave diminishing or negative returns, especially for smaller models. Authors suggest early hypothesis diversification (for example tree-of-thought). The 48,000-scenario figure came from a search summary, not the text.
quote: Since our goal is to isolate reasoning in the RCA task, we therefore restrict to single-fault scenarios.
limits: Single-fault only, so it cannot show how accuracy changes with a cap on fault size. Exact accuracy table not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no one has varied the fault-count cap for LLMs. This study also shows the cap is assumed (single fault) rather than tested. Anchoring and failure to update belief are the same failure that the HS-DAG reopen rule is meant to prevent.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) D-Bot: Database Diagnosis System using Large Language Models
finding: The authors state that single-LLM diagnosis struggles with anomalies that have multiple root causes and added a multi-LLM cross-review mode. Evidence in the text read is qualitative.
numbers: No fault-count breakdown extracted from the text read.
limits: System paper with its own benchmark; no controlled test of single-fault vs multi-fault accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: weak indication that multi-cause cases are harder for a single LLM pass and that independent review helps (same direction as AgentLocate's evaluators).

source: Search for LLM-written unsat cores and their minimality (2026 web search, summary only)
finding: One web search found no paper that measures how often LLM-written conflicts or unsat cores are non-minimal. Standard practice is to check unsatisfiability with a solver and then test each element for removal.
limits: Search summary only; a paper outside the search index could exist. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv APIs were rate-limited this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. We must build the measurement: solver-check each agent-written contradiction for subset-minimality.

source: Search for LLM plus MARCO or MUS enumeration plus hitting sets as a verifier (2026 web searches, summary only)
finding: Two searches found no paper that uses MARCO or MUS enumeration with hitting sets as an LLM verifier. Closest were Delta1-LLM (d05) and HyMUSE (d06). The SafeMin 42.1% figure from the earlier run was not re-found and stays unverified.
limits: Negative search result from snippets; not exhaustive.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays mostly open: the idea is novel in the literature seen.

source: Search for hitting-set tree variants run by LLM agents, DynamicHS replication outside the Rodler group, and carried vs restated suspect lists (2026, API budget exhausted)
finding: No outside replication of DynamicHS and no LLM study of carrying versus restating a suspect list was found within the limited search budget.
limits: Not exhaustive: Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, arXiv API returned HTTP 429.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5 and 7 stay open; need our own test.

source: Xia et al. (2026) Who Broke the System? Failure Localization in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems (AgentLocate) - counterfactual and template baselines
finding: AgentLocate authors say counterfactual replay (AgenTracer) is unstable because changing one step changes later prompts and tool outcomes. This limits replay-based 'drop one suspect and re-run' tests for agents.
numbers: On Who&When Algorithm-Generated with Qwen-7B all-at-once: AgenTracer 45.24% agent-level, AgentLocate 69.05% (table text partly garbled in extraction; other baselines not recorded).
limits: Only the 69.05% and 45.24% figures are reliable from the extracted text.
agent_relevance: In hitting-set terms, re-running with a suspect removed is a noisy consistency test for an agent, so conflicts built from replays may often be non-minimal or wrong (links to gap 2).
